summary: The note describes how the rural community of Greendale links nutrition to mental health, drawing on a dietitian, a psychiatrist, farmers, a health coach and a baker. It covers the gut-brain axis, brain-supporting nutrients, mindful eating, healthier comfort foods, harvest festivals, and a November 2023 educational campaign with weekly support groups. It concludes that local fresh produce, seasonal eating and community ties can support mental well-being.
one_line: Greendale, a rural community, uses local fresh food, mindful eating, education and support groups to help manage mental health conditions through nutrition.
key_facts: Sarah Jennings, a registered dietitian from Greendale, shared insights on diet and mental well-being in late September 2023, saying: "You are not only what you eat, but also how you feel."
Dr. Harold Thompson, a psychiatrist specializing in nutritional psychology, said on October 5, 2023 that "The gut-brain axis is our biological highway of communication."
Greendale holds a farmer market bi-weekly in its central square.
Farmer Johnathan Doe says squashes and leafy greens contain vitamins, minerals and antioxidants that can help fight inflammation associated with depression and anxiety.
Nutrients named as critical for brain health are omega-3 fatty acids, B vitamins, vitamin D, magnesium and tryptophan.
Tryptophan is found in poultry grazing on Greendale's pastures and is a precursor to serotonin, a mood-boosting neurotransmitter.
Health coach Amelia Wilson taught a workshop on "mindful eating" in early October 2023 and encourages gardening and visiting local farms.
Martha O'Connor, owner of the local bakery, uses whole grains, nuts, seeds, and local honey or maple syrup instead of refined sugars in her baked goods.
Fall festivals such as harvest celebrations, pumpkin picking and corn mazes strengthen social ties, which are essential to mental health.
Greendale launched an educational campaign on November 3, 2023 on diet and mental health, with workshops led by experts like Sarah Jennings and Dr. Harold Thompson.
Support groups for people with mental health conditions meet weekly, often over meals prepared with local produce.
Michael Anderson, a farmer who suffered from anxiety, said changing his diet and joining the group made him feel more in control, though "it's not a cure-all."
Greendale residents reported improved sleep patterns and mood stability when eating seasonally.
